**Database Schema — Document-Oriented Model**  
![][image1]   
The KilosUnlad persistence layer is implemented in MongoDB 6.0 and structured around six primary collections: users, beneficiaries, external\_records, verification\_tasks, audit\_logs, and system\_configs. Each collection is defined by a Mongoose schema with strict: true enforcement, ensuring that documents not conforming to the declared shape are rejected at the ODM layer.  
**Embedding strategy.** Where data belongs exclusively to one parent entity and is never queried independently, it is stored as a nested sub-document rather than as a separate collection. This is reflected in the ERD by sub-schemas rendered inside their parent boxes. Examples include head\_of\_household, address, demographics, and risk\_assessment within beneficiaries; power\_utility, water\_utility, telecom\_registry, transport\_registry, and landbank\_telemetry within external\_records; and field\_findings and admin\_resolution within verification\_tasks. Each sub-schema is declared with { \_id: false, strict: true } to suppress MongoDB's automatic \_id injection into nested objects and to enforce sub-level field validation.

**Referential strategy**. Cross-collection relationships fall into two categories.  
The first is **enforced references**, implemented using Mongoose ObjectId with a ref declaration. These are:

* verification\_tasks.assigned\_worker\_id → users.\_id  
* verification\_tasks.admin\_resolution.reviewed\_by → users.\_id

The second is **application-level string references,** used when the target is a natural key rather than a MongoDB \_id. These are:

* verification\_tasks.household\_id → beneficiaries.household\_id  
* external\_records.matched\_household\_id → beneficiaries.household\_id


These references are not enforced by MongoDB or Mongoose; they are maintained by the backend controllers and validated against the existence of the target natural key at write time. This design was chosen deliberately: household\_id is the domain's stable business identifier, whereas \_id is an implementation detail of MongoDB. Referencing the natural key keeps the schema portable and prevents orphaned references if a beneficiary document is ever archived.

**Audit log chain.** The audit\_logs collection is a self-referencing hash chain. Each document stores a sequence\_index (unique), a previous\_entry\_hash (the entry\_hash of the prior entry), and its own computed entry\_hash. The first entry in the chain uses a genesis hash of 64 zeros. This relationship is represented in the ERD as a self-referential one-to-zero-or-one association on audit\_logs. The chain is verified by the backend's hashChain.service.js, which recomputes each hash using canonical JSON serialization and compares it against the recorded value. Any tampering with a historical entry breaks the chain at the modified sequence\_index.

Within the audit entry, actor.user\_id is stored as a String, not as an ObjectId reference to users. This is intentional. Audit records are required to survive user deletion; a ref: 'User' constraint would produce orphaned references if the referenced user was removed. Storing the raw identifier preserves the historical fact that the action occurred without coupling the audit ledger to the mutable users collection.

Similarly, audit\_logs.target\_entity is a generic sub-schema containing a collection\_name and an entity\_id. It is not a fixed foreign key. Audit entries can reference any collection in the database (beneficiaries, verification\_tasks, system\_configs, and so on), so a polymorphic reference is required.

**Indexes.** Uniqueness constraints and query performance are enforced through MongoDB indexes declared in both the Mongoose schemas and the container initialization script (docker/mongo/init-mongo.js). Unique indexes exist on users.username, users.email, beneficiaries.household\_id, beneficiaries.head\_of\_household.national\_id, external\_records.matched\_household\_id, verification\_tasks.task\_id, audit\_logs.sequence\_index, audit\_logs.entry\_hash, and system\_configs.config\_key. A geospatial 2dsphere index is declared on beneficiaries.address.coordinates to support proximity queries. A compound index on beneficiaries.risk\_assessment.is\_flagged and address.municipality supports the administrative triage query. A compound index on verification\_tasks.assigned\_worker\_id and task\_status supports the field worker's assigned-task feed.

**Access control.** The application connects to the database as app\_user, a MongoDB account bound to the custom role kilosUnladAppRole. For five of the six collections, the role grants find, insert, update, remove, and createIndex. For audit\_logs, the role grants only find, insert, createIndex, and listIndexes. Update and delete operations on the audit ledger are blocked at the database engine level, independent of application code. This is the primary integrity guarantee of the forensic audit trail.

**Database Schema — Conceptual (Normalized) View**  
![][image2]   
The normalized conceptual model presents the same six collections decomposed to third normal form (3NF), where every embedded sub-schema is rendered as an independent entity with its own primary key. This view is presented alongside the document-oriented model to make the underlying entity relationships explicit and to demonstrate that the schema satisfies standard relational normalization criteria even though it is physically implemented as a document store.

**Primary entities**. Six entities form the backbone of the model:

* users — system accounts with role-based access control  
* beneficiaries — 4Ps household records  
* external\_records — cross-referenced utility, telecom, transport, and LandBank telemetry  
* verification\_tasks — field investigation tickets dispatched to case workers  
* audit\_logs — append-only cryptographic hash chain  
* system\_configs — runtime configuration, feature flags, and calamity moratorium zones

**Decomposed sub-entities.** Where the document model embeds data, the normalized model extracts it into a dependent entity with a one-to-one or one-to-many relationship to its parent:

* users → user\_jurisdictions (1:1). Jurisdiction is a value object scoped to a single user.  
* beneficiaries → head\_of\_household (1:1), addresses (1:1), demographics (1:1), risk\_assessments (1:1), children\_registry (1:N).  
* risk\_assessments → trigger\_badges (1:N). Badges are an unbounded array of audit reason codes.  
* external\_records → power\_utility (1:1), water\_utility (1:1), telecom\_registry (1:1), landbank\_telemetry (1:1), and vehicles (1:N). Vehicles were extracted from the transport\_registry object because they form a nested array within it.  
* verification\_tasks → field\_findings (1:1) and admin\_resolutions (1:1). The two are separated because they are populated at different stages of the task lifecycle: field\_findings at submission, admin\_resolutions at review.  
* field\_findings → livelihood\_asset\_verification (1:1), landbank\_card\_inspection (1:1), client\_geolocation (1:1), and evidence\_attachments (1:N).  
* evidence\_attachments → exif\_metadata (1:1). EXIF data is captured per photo and belongs to exactly one attachment.  
* audit\_logs → audit\_actors (1:1), audit\_target\_entities (1:1), audit\_state\_deltas (0:1). The actor, target, and delta are separated for clarity.  
* system\_configs → calamity\_moratorium\_zones (1:N), threshold\_configs (1:1), feature\_flags (1:1).

**Primary and foreign keys.** In the normalized view:

* Every root entity has a surrogate primary key \_id (ObjectId).  
* Every dependent sub-entity inherits its parent's identifier as a foreign key and is marked PK in the model because the combination of (parent\_id, natural\_key) is unique within its scope. For example, children\_registry.beneficiary\_id is marked PK because child records are identified by their parent plus their own birthdate, not by a surrogate \_id.  
* Unique business keys are marked UK: household\_id, task\_id, username, email, national\_id, config\_key, sequence\_index, entry\_hash, matched\_household\_id, plate\_number (per vehicle), and coordinates (as a GeoJSON point).  
* Cross-entity foreign keys are marked FK:  
* verification\_tasks.assigned\_worker\_id → users.\_id  
* verification\_tasks.admin\_resolution.reviewed\_by → users.\_id  
* verification\_tasks.household\_id → beneficiaries.household\_id (soft)  
* external\_records.matched\_household\_id → beneficiaries.household\_id (soft)  
* audit\_actors.user\_id → users.\_id (logical only; not enforced)

**Relationship cardinality.** The model declares the following cardinalities:

| Relationship | Cardinality |
| :---- | :---- |
| users → verification\_tasks (as assigned worker) | 1:N |
| users → verification\_tasks (as reviewing admin) | 1:N |
| beneficiaries → external\_records | 1:0..1 (soft) |
| beneficiaries → verification\_tasks | 1:N (soft) |
| verification\_tasks → field\_findings | 1:0..1 |
| verification\_tasks → admin\_resolutions | 1:0..1 |
| field\_findings → evidence\_attachments | 1:N |
| audit\_logs → audit\_logs (self-referential) | 1:0..1 |
| system\_configs → calamity\_moratorium\_zones | 1:N |

**Referential integrity.** Two classes of reference are distinguished:

1. **Enforced by Mongoose *ref*.** MongoDB stores the referenced ObjectId; Mongoose does not enforce existence at write time, but the backend controllers validate the target before persisting. These references are: assigned\_worker\_id, admin\_resolution.reviewed\_by.  
2. **Logical, not enforced.** These are string references maintained by the backend. They are validated at write time by controller logic but are not declared as ref in the schema. This is intentional to preserve historical records and to allow flexible cross-collection joins. These references are: household\_id, matched\_household\_id, actor.user\_id, and the generic target\_entity.entity\_id.

**Why the physical model departs from 3NF.** MongoDB's document store deliberately denormalizes related data into the same document when that data is always accessed together. The normalized view presented here represents the logical data model; the document model (Style A) represents the physical implementation. The two are consistent: every sub-entity in the normalized view corresponds to a sub-schema in the document view, and every foreign key in the normalized view corresponds to either a Mongoose ref or an application-level reference in the document view.

**Normalization note.** The document schema satisfies 1NF (atomic leaf values, arrays for repeating groups), 2NF (no partial dependencies; every sub-entity has a single parent), and 3NF (no transitive dependencies; identifiers such as household\_id and national\_id are stored at the level where they are functionally determined). The only departure from strict relational practice is the deliberate embedding of sub-schemas, which is a recognized and accepted pattern in document-oriented databases when the embedded data is bounded and always accessed with its parent.
